name: United Arab Emirates
summary: Bringing a casket into the UAE goes through the UAE embassy or consulate in the country of death, which attests the death certificate and its Arabic translation; detailed import rules for non-nationals are not published, so confirm with the consulate. Leaving the UAE requires police no-objection letters, an attested death certificate, embalming and the home embassy's no-objection letter.
documents: Death certificate attested by the country of death and by the UAE embassy, with certified Arabic translation (official u.ae list for UAE nationals)
Report on the cause of death (UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs, for UAE nationals)
Embalming certificate and certificate of sealed casket (expected; confirm with the consulate)
Copy of the deceased's passport and airway bill
coffin: No official UAE import standard for the casket was found. Use a hermetically sealed, zinc-lined casket in an outer wooden case meeting IATA/airline requirements; confirm with the UAE consulate.
embalming: Embalming is required for remains leaving the UAE (gov.uk). For incoming remains, embalming is expected but not confirmed by an official UAE source.
consular: For UAE nationals who die abroad, the UAE embassy in the country of death attests the death certificate and translates it into Arabic. For non-UAE nationals being buried in the UAE, confirm requirements with the UAE consulate.
arrival: No official arrival procedure was found. The receiving funeral service collects the casket after customs and health clearance; Muslim burials are normally held very quickly. Local burial needs a burial permit from the police (u.ae).
private_aviation: No official rule specific to private or charter flights carrying human remains was found for the UAE. Remains are cleared like air cargo: plan arrival at an international airport with customs and health staff, and have the handling agent and the receiving funeral home confirm clearance before departure.
private_jet_note: Confirm cargo and customs clearance of the casket with the handling agent at the UAE arrival airport.
export: The death must be registered and an official death certificate issued; MOFA stamps and signs the certificate and its translation. Police issue no-objection letters (to the airport police, embalming facility and mortuary). The deceased's embassy issues a no-objection letter and cancels the passport; the residency visa is cancelled. The body must be embalmed and placed in a coffin meeting specific rules; documents travel with the body (with seven photocopies each for the cargo handler). Cremation is possible. Typical delay is a few days, longer if a forensic report is needed.
export_points: Death certificate stamped by the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs
Police no-objection letters for mortuary, embalming and airport
Embassy no-objection letter and cancelled passport
Embalming certificate; seven copies of each document

name: Saudi Arabia
summary: No official Saudi procedure for importing a casket was found; expect the death certificate to be legalised by the Saudi embassy and translated into Arabic, and confirm with the consulate. Sending remains out of Saudi Arabia is slow: sponsor-led, with embassy NOC, governorate and police approvals and mandatory embalming, usually 3 to 6 weeks.
documents: Death certificate, legalised by the destination country's embassy/consulate and translated into Arabic (confirm with the consulate)
Medical certificate stating the death was not due to a contagious disease (confirm with the consulate)
Embalming certificate (confirm with the consulate)
Certificate of hermetic sealing of the casket (confirm with the consulate)
Copy of the deceased's passport and airway bill
coffin: No official Saudi import standard was found. Use a hermetically sealed, zinc-lined casket in an outer wooden case meeting airline requirements; confirm with the Saudi consulate.
embalming: Embalming is mandatory before remains leave Saudi Arabia (British Embassy Riyadh). For incoming remains, embalming is expected but not confirmed officially.
consular: Documents are normally legalised by the Saudi embassy or consulate in the country of death. Specific import requirements are not published; confirm with the consulate.
arrival: No official arrival procedure was found. Burial options for non-Muslims in Saudi Arabia are very limited (not confirmed by an official source; check with the consulate). Muslim burial normally takes place very quickly; government offices are closed Friday and Saturday.
private_aviation: No official rule specific to private or charter flights carrying human remains was found for Saudi Arabia. Remains are cleared like air cargo: plan arrival at an international airport with customs and health staff, and have the handling agent and the receiving funeral home confirm clearance before departure.
private_jet_note: Confirm customs clearance of the casket and the receiving funeral service before departure.
export: The sponsor/employer drives the process. The deceased's embassy issues a no-objection certificate (after the next of kin's consent or power of attorney). The city Principality/Governorate instructs police, who issue letters to the mortuary, passport office (exit visa), cargo and customs. A 'Death Certificate for Non-Saudis' is issued by the Civil Affairs office; documents are attested by the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Embalming is mandatory, done at a government hospital mortuary about 12 hours before departure, with an embalming certificate and letter to the airline. The body goes to the cargo office 6 to 12 hours before departure. Typical delay 3 to 6 weeks; months for unnatural deaths.
export_points: Sponsor handles the process; embassy NOC first
Governorate and police permission, final exit visa
Mandatory embalming at a government mortuary
Typically 3 to 6 weeks, longer if investigated

name: Kuwait
summary: No official Kuwaiti procedure for importing a casket was found; confirm with the Kuwaiti embassy. Sending remains out of Kuwait requires prosecutor and police permission, a Certificate of Repatriation from the Preventive Medicine Unit and a sealed shipping container; embalming is not available in Kuwait.

coffin: No official Kuwaiti import standard was found. Use a hermetically sealed casket in an outer case meeting airline requirements; confirm with the Kuwaiti consulate.
embalming: Embalming and cremation are not available in Kuwait (against Islamic law and custom, per British Embassy guidance). Whether embalming is required for incoming remains is not published.
consular: Not published; confirm legalisation and Arabic translation with the Kuwaiti embassy or consulate. Kuwaiti documents must be attested by the Kuwait Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
arrival: No official arrival procedure was found. Burial is not permitted after sunset; government offices are closed Friday and Saturday with no emergency service.

Remains are cleared like air cargo: plan arrival at an international airport with customs and health staff, and have the handling agent and the receiving funeral home confirm clearance before departure.

export: Register the death at the Central Registry (Hawalli or Ahmadi); the certificate is attested by the Kuwait MOFA and translated. The Preventive Medicine Department must complete tests and the Prosecutor must authorise release; police issue a repatriation permit. The Preventive Medicine Unit at Al-Sabah Hospital issues a Certificate of Repatriation and transfer authorisation; the General Department of Criminal Evidence is notified. Al-Sabah Hospital Mortuary is the only facility preparing remains for shipment. No embalming: the body goes in a sealed shipping container; the shipping agent witnesses casketing and an embassy representative applies the seal on shipment day. Post-mortem reports take 3 to 4 weeks.

name: Jordan
summary: A foreign death certificate for a Jordanian must be attested by the Jordanian embassy (or MOFA route) and translated into Arabic by a certified centre; detailed casket import rules are not published, so confirm with the Jordanian consulate. Leaving Jordan requires the home embassy's no-objection letter and next-of-kin consent; burial is normally within 24 hours.

embalming: Not published officially for incoming remains; confirm with the consulate. Infectious conditions (such as hepatitis or HIV) must be declared to the authorities.
consular: The Jordanian embassy or consulate attests the foreign death certificate; the death of a Jordanian can be registered with the Civil Status and Passports Department or at a Jordanian embassy (JD1 fee, extra JD10 after 7 days).
arrival: Burial is required within 24 hours of death; a Ministry of Health permit can extend this to 72 hours if remains are kept in a suitable facility (gov.uk). Cremation is not permitted in Jordan.

Embalming and sealing requirements for exit are not published officially. Cremation is not permitted.
